doc.title: Ignacio Berroa interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 22, 2021 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Father's embrace of and break with Castro's revolution
summary: Berroa says his father fought at the Bay of Pigs, then turned against Castro around 1965 because the promises proved lies.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: I wanted to just follow up on your early life. And you had said your father was a fan of Castro and fought in the Bay of Pigs and embraced the political situation at the time, is that correct?

Yes. Like millions of Cubans, they embraced the Cuban revolution, I mean coming from a poor family so rightfully so my father was in Castro’s eyes because all of the promises that Castro made to the poor Cuban people, talking about equality, inclusion, and so forth and so on. So anyway, yes he did. He fought on Bay of Pigs and then around 1965 he went the opposite way. So he abandoned Castro’s revolution.
What specifically did he get disenchanted with?

At some point, I was a kid but at some point and then later on we found that most, almost all of Castro’s promises were lies, that he was lying. He was lying to the Cuban people. I don’t know, I don’t know if he was an egomaniac, I don’t know if he did that on purpose, but most of the promises were lies. And you know I don’t want to get too much into politics, because I know that a lot of people here in the United States and in the world that are Castro’s fans, and they think that Castro’s policies of the Castro revolution was the best that could have happened to the Cuban people. But just a reflection — if Castro’s revolution was so great why so many people abandoned the island, in rafts — why so many Cubans tried to leave the island, why 125,000 people arrived here to the United States in 1980 if the country is so great. So that’s my point of view on this. You know it’s like I’m going to put you an analogy, what people, I always do this analogy people who compare capitalism, which is not the greatest system in the world either, but they compare capitalism to socialism. So I always say well I’m 68 years old so I have witnessed quite a few Olympic games. I have never seen any athlete from any of the poorest countries in the world that compete in the Olympic games when those games have been celebrated in socialist countries like the former Soviet Union or Hungary or anyplace, I’ve never seen any of those people asking for political asylum in those
